screens.title: Introduction to Templates: Generic Programming
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore templates — the C++ mechanism for generic programming that removes repetitive, type-specific code. You will learn what templates are, why they solve the common problem of copying the same logic for different types, and how the compiler generates concrete functions and classes from those blueprints. We begin by motivating the problem: imagine writing separate swap or stack types for every data type you use. Templates allow you to write a single blueprint with placeholders like T or U, and then the compiler instantiates the concrete versions for the types you actually use. You will see both function templates and class templates, understand template instantiation, and learn practical pitfalls such as linker errors when definitions are separated incorrectly. By the end of the chapter you will be ready to implement reusable utilities like a generic Pair class and to use standard library templates such as vectors and maps with confidence. Consider how a single template can replace multiple nearly-identical functions — that economy is the core benefit. Are you ready to reduce duplication and write more reusable C++?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Templates let you write a single function or class blueprint with type placeholders. The compiler generates concrete versions when you use them with specific types, avoiding duplication.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Introduction to Templates
Introduction to Templates: Generic Programming
Write type-agnostic code once and reuse it safely across types.
Orientation

Templates are blueprints with placeholder types like T or U. The compiler fills in these placeholders to create concrete functions and classes. This reduces duplicated code and improves maintainability.

You will learn function templates, class templates, instantiation rules, and common linker pitfalls. Practical examples include a swap function, a stack class, and a Pair activity.

Explore Key Topics
Function Templates
Write one function blueprint to handle many types, e.g., a generic swap.
Class Templates
Design type-agnostic containers like a Stack or Pair using templates.
Common Pitfalls
Understand instantiation and why separating definitions can cause linker errors.
Concept Map
Templates act as blueprints. When used, the compiler creates concrete code for the types you supply. Think of a template as a mold that can produce many type-specific parts.
Blueprints → Instantiation → Concrete types
In this lesson
  • Why templates remove duplication and improve reuse.
  • How to write function and class templates with examples.
  • Common compilation and linker pitfalls and how to avoid them.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide your learning: first, you will understand the concept of generic programming and why templates matter. That means recognizing patterns where logic is identical but types differ and seeing how a template removes duplication. Second, you'll be able to implement function templates, writing a single template that the compiler will instantiate for various types. For example, you will write a generic swap function and use it with integers and floating-point values. Third, you'll implement class templates to build type-agnostic data structures like a simple stack or the Pair activity, and you'll test instantiations such as Stack of integers and Stack of strings. Fourth, you'll identify common template issues that appear at compile or link time, most notably linker errors caused by separating template definitions improperly. For each objective you'll practice with small examples and check your understanding by predicting compiler behavior. These competencies prepare you for using and creating reusable libraries and for understanding the Standard Template Library. Keep these goals in mind as you move through the lessons and the Pair hands-on activity.

screens.title: Why Generic Programming?
screens.narratorSegment: Generic programming is a paradigm where algorithms and structures are written without binding to a specific concrete type. The central claim is simple: when the logic of a function or class is identical across types, we should write one implementation that works for all types. A common motivating example is writing separate maximum or swap functions for ints and doubles — that leads to duplicated code and higher maintenance cost. A template abstracts the type using a placeholder such as T. Because the algorithm remains the same, you gain reuse, fewer bugs, and clearer intent. Concretely, a swap template uses T to let the compiler generate swap for int or double when those types are used. A useful misconception check: templates are not a runtime polymorphism mechanism. They do not use virtual dispatch or inheritance; instead, the compiler produces concrete type-specific code at compile time. This means templates can be faster, but also that the compiler must see the template definition before it can instantiate it. Key takeaway: generic programming reduces duplication and produces type-specific code via compile-time instantiation, but it is not the same as runtime polymorphism. How could you spot places in your code where multiple overloads become a single template?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Generic programming writes algorithms independent of concrete types so a single blueprint can handle many type instantiations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Why Generic Programming?
Problem: duplication

When logic repeats across types, separate implementations create maintenance and correctness risks. Generic programming replaces many similar functions with one parametrized blueprint.

Analogy
A template is like a mold for shoes: one mold can make many sizes. The mold holds the process; the size parameter produces the concrete shoe.
Common misconception
Templates are not runtime polymorphism. They generate distinct code for each type at compile time rather than dispatching at runtime.
Key Takeaway

Find repeated logic across types and convert it to a template to reduce duplication and bugs while keeping performance.

Where it helps
  • Utility functions like swap or max used for multiple numeric types.
  • Containers such as stacks, vectors, and maps that hold various element types.
  • Library code that must be reused across projects and types.
Example snapshot
If you have swap for int and swap for double, convert both into a single template that accepts a placeholder type. The compiler will generate swap<int> or swap<double> automatically when used.

screens.title: Template Syntax and the typename Keyword
screens.narratorSegment: The basic template declaration uses the syntax template<typename T> or template<class T> to introduce a type parameter. This line tells the compiler that T is a placeholder for a type, not a variable or a value. A clear definition: template declares parameters that stand for types or values. Use typename when defining a type parameter — it is more semantically accurate, although class is allowed for historical reasons. For example, template<typename T> void swap(T& a, T& b) declares a single type parameter named T and defines a generic swap. A common confusion is thinking typename implies dynamic typing; it does not. It simply labels the parameter as a type at compile time. Another misconception is mixing type and non-type parameters; templates can accept values too, but when you see typename T you should expect type substitution. Concrete example: when you call swap with two ints, the compiler generates a concrete swap where T is int. Takeaway: template<typename T> defines a compile-time placeholder for a type and is the starting point for writing general functions or classes. Try replacing typename with class in examples to see identical behavior in most cases.

keyIdea.title: Syntax
keyIdea.text: Use template<typename T> to declare a type parameter. 'typename' marks the placeholder as a type known at compile time.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Template Syntax
template<typename T>

The template declaration introduces a type parameter. It signals that the following function or class is generic and that the compiler should replace the placeholder with concrete types at instantiation.

Note on 'class' vs 'typename'
Using class instead of typename for a type parameter is permitted, but typename is clearer when the parameter represents a type rather than a user-defined class only.
Concrete example
<?cpp
template <typename T>
void swap(T& a, T& b) {
  T temp = a;
  a = b;
  b = temp;
}
?>
When called with ints, the compiler creates swap<int>.
Misconception check
typename does not change runtime behavior. Templates are resolved at compile time; typename only labels a parameter as a type during compilation.

screens.title: Function Templates: swap Example
screens.narratorSegment: A function template demonstrates templates in a compact, practical way. Consider a generic swap. The template declaration template<typename T> introduces T as the type parameter. The function body uses T just as a concrete type would. When you call swap with two integers, the compiler generates a swap where T is int. When you call it with doubles, it generates another version for double. Concrete example: the swap template assigns a temporary of type T and exchanges values. A common error is trying to swap values of different types in one call; the compiler cannot deduce a single T when argument types differ. You would then need overloads or explicit template arguments, or write a templated function that accepts two type parameters. Another practical point: function templates often have arguments deduced from function calls, which makes usage concise. Misconception check: template instantiation is performed only for the types you use; unused template forms are not generated, which keeps code size practical. Closing question: if you need to swap an int and a double in one call, what limitation of templates will you need to address?

keyIdea.title: Function template example
keyIdea.text: A single template function can replace many type-specific overloads; template argument deduction creates concrete versions when called.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Function Templates
Generic swap

This template swaps two values of the same deduced type. The compiler will generate a separate swap function for each distinct type you use.

<?cpp
template <typename T>
void swap(T& a, T& b) {
  T temp = a;
  a = b;
  b = temp;
}

int main() {
  int x = 1, y = 2;
  swap(x, y); // compiler instantiates swap<int>
  double p = 1.5, q = 2.5;
  swap(p, q); // compiler instantiates swap<double>
}
?>
When deduction fails
If you call swap(1, 2.0) the compiler cannot deduce a single T because argument types differ. You must use explicit template parameters or overloads to handle mixed types.
Quick tips
  • Rely on argument deduction for concise calls.
  • Use multiple template parameters when types differ.
  • Keep template bodies visible at instantiation sites.
Key Takeaway

Function templates let you write one generic function; the compiler auto-generates concrete versions where needed. Watch for deduction limits when argument types differ.

screens.title: Class Templates: Building a Generic Stack
screens.narratorSegment: Class templates let you define entire data structures that work for any element type. The provided MyStack example shows the pattern: template<typename T> class MyStack {... } creates a blueprint. Inside you can use T for member types, arrays, and return values. When you write MyStack<int> intStack(10); the compiler generates a class with int substituted for T. A concrete example in the source shows dynamic allocation of T array elements and push, pop, peek operations. Remember to handle default construction when returning T() from pop on underflow: this relies on T being default-constructible. A common pitfall is assuming all types used with a template will support particular operations; for example, pushing a type that cannot be copied will break code that copies T. Also note that separating member function definitions into a. cpp file will prevent the compiler from instantiating methods at the call site, leading to linker errors. Practice by instantiating MyStack for int and for std::string; you will see how the same blueprint yields two concrete classes. Takeaway: class templates give you powerful reusable containers, but you must consider type requirements and keep definitions available for instantiation.

keyIdea.title: Class template pattern
keyIdea.text: Declare class templates with template<typename T>. Use T for member variables and methods; instantiate with MyStack<int> or MyStack<std::string>.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Class Templates
MyStack<T> example

Use a template parameter T for the element type. The stack allocates a T array and provides push, pop, and peek. Instantiations like MyStack<int> and MyStack<std::string> create concrete classes.

<?cpp
template <typename T>
class MyStack {
private:
  T* arr;
  int top;
  int capacity;
public:
  MyStack(int size) : capacity(size), top(-1) { arr = new T[capacity]; }
  ~MyStack() { delete[] arr; }
  void push(const T& val) { arr[++top] = val; }
  T pop() { if(top==-1){ return T(); } return arr[top--]; }
};
?>
Type requirements
Templates may require that types support copying, default construction, or certain operators. If a type lacks these, the instantiation will fail at the point it is used.
Practical check
Instantiate MyStack<int> and MyStack<std::string> in a small main to verify push/pop behavior and to test exception or underflow handling.
Key Takeaway

Class templates let you design reusable containers, but check the expectations you place on types and keep definitions visible for instantiation.

screens.title: Instantiation: Template vs Regular Class
screens.narratorSegment: Template instantiation is the process where the compiler generates concrete functions or classes from a generic template using the types you supply. Contrast this with a regular class: a non-template class has a single compiled form that the linker uses. For templates, the compiler waits until it knows which types you used and then produces a version for each unique set of template arguments. For example, using MyStack<int> and MyStack<std::string> produces two distinct classes at compile time. An important subtlety: the template definition must be visible when the compiler instantiates it; otherwise you get undefined reference or linker errors because the compiler couldn't generate the needed symbols. Another difference is code bloat risk — each instantiation produces separate code — but that is balanced by type safety and often better inlining. Misconception check: instantiation is not a runtime action; it happens during compilation. Practical takeaway: keep template definitions in headers and be deliberate about which instantiations you create to manage compile time and binary size. Instantiation: Template vs Regular Class means the compiler produces a concrete version of a template for each distinct set of template arguments used in code, at compile time.. In practical terms, how the compiler generates concrete code from templates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation explained
keyIdea.text: The compiler produces a concrete version of a template for each distinct set of template arguments used in code, at compile time.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Template Instantiation
Instantiated vs single class
A template yields separate compiled versions for each type you use. A regular class has one compiled version shared by all uses. Instantiation happens at compile time and requires visible definitions.
Example
Using MyStack<int> and MyStack<std::string> produces two concrete classes in the final binary generated by the compiler.
Consequences
  • Each instantiation generates code, which can increase binary size.
  • Instantiation gives type-specific optimizations and inlining opportunities.
  • Definitions must be visible at instantiation to avoid linker errors.
Misconception

Templates are not polymorphic at runtime. Instantiation happens at compile time and produces distinct code paths for each type used.

screens.title: Linker Errors with Templates
screens.narratorSegment: One frequent pitfall is getting undefined reference linker errors when templates are declared in a header but defined in a separate. cpp file. The fundamental reason is that templates are instantiated where they are used, and the compiler must see the full template definition at that point to generate the concrete code. If only a declaration is visible, the compiler cannot produce the necessary instantiation and the linker cannot find the symbol. For beginners the simplest and most reliable solution is to place both declaration and definition in the header file so that any translation unit that uses the template has access to the full definition. Alternatives include explicit instantiation or including the. cpp at the bottom of the header, but these are more advanced techniques. A concrete scenario: you declare a LinkedList template in LinkedList. h but implement member functions in LinkedList. cpp. When main. cpp uses LinkedList, the compiler will not instantiate the methods because their definitions were not visible; the final link step reports undefined references. Misconception check: this is not a runtime bug — it is a compile/link-time visibility problem. Takeaway: keep template definitions available at the point of instantiation, typically by defining templates in headers.

keyIdea.title: Linker error cause
keyIdea.text: Linker errors occur when the compiler cannot see template definitions at instantiation time; the usual fix is to place definitions in the header.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Linker Errors
Undefined reference from separated definitions

When template definitions live in a .cpp, other translation units cannot see them to instantiate concrete code. The linker then fails to find the needed symbols and reports undefined references.

Beginners' fix:
Move template definitions into the header file so the compiler can instantiate templates wherever they are used.
Concrete scenario
LinkedList.h declares the template; LinkedList.cpp defines members. main.cpp uses LinkedList<int>. Because main.cpp can't see the definitions, the compiler cannot instantiate functions and the linker reports undefined references.
Practical tip

Keep template code in headers or use explicit instantiation techniques only when you understand the build system implications.

screens.title: Type Deduction and When to Specify Types
screens.narratorSegment: Type deduction is the compiler's ability to infer template arguments from function call parameters. For many function templates you simply call the function and the compiler deduces the types automatically. For example, calling printValue(5) lets the compiler deduce T as int. However, deduction has limits. If argument types differ or if the call lacks enough information, the compiler cannot deduce a single type parameter and you must specify template arguments manually. For instance, a swap template requires both parameters to be the same deduced type; swap(1, 2.0) fails deduction. Another case is class templates where you must provide the type when you declare the object: MyStack s(10); here no deduction happens at the point of declaration. A common misconception is that deduction will magically convert or coerce types; it will not. It must find a single type that matches parameter types or you must supply explicit template parameters. Practical advice: rely on deduction for concise calls, but when you need mixed types or more control, declare explicit template arguments or use multiple template parameters. Question to consider: what rules guide the compiler's deduction when references, constness, or pointers are present?

keyIdea.title: Deduction rules
keyIdea.text: The compiler deduces template types from function arguments when possible. When arguments conflict or are missing, you must specify types explicitly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Type Deduction
How deduction works

The compiler inspects function call arguments and matches them to template parameters to infer types. This reduces verbosity but has clear limits when types differ or when context is missing.

Example
printValue(5) → T deduced as int. swap(1, 2.0) → deduction fails because a single T cannot match both int and double.
When to specify types
  • When argument types differ and a single type cannot be deduced.
  • When you declare a class template object — explicit type arguments are required.
  • When you want to force a particular overload or conversion path.
Misconception

Type deduction will not silently convert differing argument types into a single type. It must find an exact match pattern to infer T.

screens.title: Template Metaprogramming: Compile-time Computation
screens.narratorSegment: Templates are more than type generalization; they can be used to compute and configure code at compile time. This style, called template metaprogramming, leverages the compiler's instantiation mechanism to evaluate simple computations or generate types during compilation. You might use templates to compute factorials or to choose an optimized implementation based on a constant parameter; these are compile-time actions that can eliminate work at runtime. A caveat for beginners: template metaprogramming can be hard to read and debug because errors surface during compilation and templates can be verbose. For day-to-day use, understand that templates enable compile-time decisions and specialization, but reserve heavy metaprogramming patterns for performance-critical code or library authorship. Misconception check: metaprogramming does not magically execute code at runtime — it moves computation and selection to the compiler phase. Takeaway: know that templates can express more than types; they can compute and shape code before your program runs, offering powerful optimization opportunities when used carefully. Template Metaprogramming: Compile-time Computation means templates can encode compile-time logic and computations, generating optimized code without runtime overhead.. In practical terms, templates can perform computations during compilation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Template Metaprogramming
Templates as compile-time tools

Beyond type generalization, templates can evaluate expressions and select code paths at compile time. This enables optimizations and compile-time checks, but increases complexity and can make errors harder to interpret.

When to use
  • When compile-time computation reduces runtime cost.
  • When choosing specialized implementations for known constants.
  • When building library code that must be type- or size-parameterized at compile time.
Misconception check
Template metaprogramming does not run at runtime. It shapes types and code during compilation so the final binary contains specialized, optimized code.
Key Takeaway

Templates can be used to compute during compilation, creating efficient, type-specific code while keeping runtime overhead low.

screens.title: Activity: Implement a Generic Pair Class
screens.narratorSegment: This guided activity consolidates class template knowledge. Your task is to implement a Pair template with two type parameters, T1 and T2. The Pair should hold first and second members, provide a constructor that initializes them, getter methods getFirst and getSecond, and a printPair method that writes both values to the console. Test your Pair with Pair<int,double> and Pair<std::string,char>. A concrete starting point is given in the chapter's starter code. Important points: place the full template definition in the header so the compiler can instantiate it where you test it. When implementing printPair, rely on operator<< being available for the types you test. A common beginner mistake is returning references to temporary objects or hiding template definitions in separate. cpp files, which leads to linker errors. After implementing, instantiate two Pair objects in main and call printPair to confirm output. Reflective question: how would you modify Pair to support types that are not streamable to standard output? screens.title: Typical Workflow with Templates
screens.narratorSegment: Adopt a predictable workflow when using templates. Step one: design the template by identifying repeated logic across types and selecting appropriate type parameters such as T or T1 and T2. Step two: implement the template in the header so the compiler can see definitions at instantiation. Step three: instantiate and test with concrete types in a small main to confirm behavior, for example testing MyStack<int> and Pair<std::string,char>. Step four: if you encounter undefined reference errors, check that definitions were not hidden in. cpp files; move definitions into the header as a beginner-friendly fix. Step five: refine type requirements by documenting whether T must be default-constructible, copyable, or streamable. A common mistake is skipping the type requirements step, causing confusing errors only when certain types are used. Another helpful step is adding small unit tests per instantiation. Takeaway: a short process loop—design, implement in header, instantiate, test, and fix—keeps template development manageable and predictable. Typical Workflow with Templates means design the template, implement it in the header, instantiate with types, test, and resolve visibility or type-requirement issues.. In practical terms, design, implement, instantiate, test, and fix linker issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Template Workflow
Step-by-step process
1. Design
Find repeated logic and choose type parameters.
2. Implement
Write full definitions in the header to allow instantiation.
3. Instantiate
Create concrete types like MyStack<int> in small tests.
4. Test
Run tests to verify behavior and type constraints.
5. Fix
Resolve linker errors or adapt type requirements as needed.
A brief checklist: ensure header visibility for definitions, document required type operations, and keep small, focused tests for each instantiation. This process reduces surprises and helps you diagnose template-specific issues quickly.
Key Takeaway

Follow a short design-implement-instantiate-test-fix loop and keep definitions in headers to avoid linker issues and unclear errors.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important ideas. First, generic programming enables writing algorithms and structures that work independently of concrete types — templates are the mechanism for this in C++. Second, a template is a blueprint that uses placeholder types like T or T1 and T2; when you use a template with specific types the compiler generates concrete code. Third, function templates let you replace many similar overloads with a single implementation, relying on template argument deduction to make calls concise. These three ideas capture the essence: abstraction of type, blueprint-based code generation, and practical reuse. Keep them in mind when you refactor duplicated type-specific code into templates. A final reflective question: which repeated functions in your codebase could become clean, well-documented templates? Key Concepts means templates let you write flexible, reusable code by abstracting types and letting the compiler generate concrete implementations.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Key Concepts
Class Template
A class parameterized by types to form type-specific classes upon instantiation.
Template Instantiation
The compile-time generation of concrete code from a template using supplied type arguments.
Linker Error (Templates)
Occurs when template definitions aren't visible at instantiation time, causing undefined references.
Quick summary

Use templates to reduce duplication, keep definitions visible, and verify type requirements early with small tests.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore templates — the C++ mechanism for generic programming that removes repetitive, type-specific code. You will learn what templates are, why they solve the common problem of copying the same logic for different types, and how the compiler generates concrete functions and classes from those blueprints. We begin by motivating the problem: imagine writing separate swap or stack types for every data type you use. Templates allow you to write a single blueprint with placeholders like T or U, and then the compiler instantiates the concrete versions for the types you actually use. You will see both function templates and class templates, understand template instantiation, and learn practical pitfalls such as linker errors when definitions are separated incorrectly. By the end of the chapter you will be ready to implement reusable utilities like a generic Pair class and to use standard library templates such as vectors and maps with confidence. Consider how a single template can replace multiple nearly-identical functions — that economy is the core benefit. Are you ready to reduce duplication and write more reusable C++?

These objectives guide your learning: first, you will understand the concept of generic programming and why templates matter. That means recognizing patterns where logic is identical but types differ and seeing how a template removes duplication. Second, you'll be able to implement function templates, writing a single template that the compiler will instantiate for various types. For example, you will write a generic swap function and use it with integers and floating-point values. Third, you'll implement class templates to build type-agnostic data structures like a simple stack or the Pair activity, and you'll test instantiations such as Stack of integers and Stack of strings. Fourth, you'll identify common template issues that appear at compile or link time, most notably linker errors caused by separating template definitions improperly. For each objective you'll practice with small examples and check your understanding by predicting compiler behavior. These competencies prepare you for using and creating reusable libraries and for understanding the Standard Template Library. Keep these goals in mind as you move through the lessons and the Pair hands-on activity.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and verification. You'll implement the Pair class activity to apply class templates and gain hands-on experience with type parameters like T1 and T2. For functions, you'll write and test a generic swap to see template argument deduction in action, and you'll observe when deduction fails so you can explicitly specify types. As you code, you'll check compiler messages to learn how the compiler indicates instantiation steps and missing definitions. We'll also include short exercises that ask you to predict output for a simple printValue template, reinforcing type deduction behavior with examples such as integers, string literals, and floats. Finally, you'll practice resolving the most common beginner linker error by moving template definitions into the header. Each practice item is paired with a verification: run a small main that instantiates templates and confirm the expected output or fix linker errors. These checks help you move from understanding to applied competence.

Generic programming is a paradigm where algorithms and structures are written without binding to a specific concrete type. The central claim is simple: when the logic of a function or class is identical across types, we should write one implementation that works for all types. A common motivating example is writing separate maximum or swap functions for ints and doubles — that leads to duplicated code and higher maintenance cost. A template abstracts the type using a placeholder such as T. Because the algorithm remains the same, you gain reuse, fewer bugs, and clearer intent. Concretely, a swap template uses T to let the compiler generate swap for int or double when those types are used. A useful misconception check: templates are not a runtime polymorphism mechanism. They do not use virtual dispatch or inheritance; instead, the compiler produces concrete type-specific code at compile time. This means templates can be faster, but also that the compiler must see the template definition before it can instantiate it. Key takeaway: generic programming reduces duplication and produces type-specific code via compile-time instantiation, but it is not the same as runtime polymorphism. How could you spot places in your code where multiple overloads become a single template?

The basic template declaration uses the syntax template<typename T> or template<class T> to introduce a type parameter. This line tells the compiler that T is a placeholder for a type, not a variable or a value. A clear definition: template declares parameters that stand for types or values. Use typename when defining a type parameter — it is more semantically accurate, although class is allowed for historical reasons. For example, template<typename T> void swap(T& a, T& b) declares a single type parameter named T and defines a generic swap. A common confusion is thinking typename implies dynamic typing; it does not. It simply labels the parameter as a type at compile time. Another misconception is mixing type and non-type parameters; templates can accept values too, but when you see typename T you should expect type substitution. Concrete example: when you call swap with two ints, the compiler generates a concrete swap where T is int. Takeaway: template<typename T> defines a compile-time placeholder for a type and is the starting point for writing general functions or classes. Try replacing typename with class in examples to see identical behavior in most cases.

A function template demonstrates templates in a compact, practical way. Consider a generic swap. The template declaration template<typename T> introduces T as the type parameter. The function body uses T just as a concrete type would. When you call swap with two integers, the compiler generates a swap where T is int. When you call it with doubles, it generates another version for double. Concrete example: the swap template assigns a temporary of type T and exchanges values. A common error is trying to swap values of different types in one call; the compiler cannot deduce a single T when argument types differ. You would then need overloads or explicit template arguments, or write a templated function that accepts two type parameters. Another practical point: function templates often have arguments deduced from function calls, which makes usage concise. Misconception check: template instantiation is performed only for the types you use; unused template forms are not generated, which keeps code size practical. Closing question: if you need to swap an int and a double in one call, what limitation of templates will you need to address?

Class templates let you define entire data structures that work for any element type. The provided MyStack example shows the pattern: template<typename T> class MyStack {... } creates a blueprint. Inside you can use T for member types, arrays, and return values. When you write MyStack<int> intStack(10); the compiler generates a class with int substituted for T. A concrete example in the source shows dynamic allocation of T array elements and push, pop, peek operations. Remember to handle default construction when returning T() from pop on underflow: this relies on T being default-constructible. A common pitfall is assuming all types used with a template will support particular operations; for example, pushing a type that cannot be copied will break code that copies T. Also note that separating member function definitions into a. cpp file will prevent the compiler from instantiating methods at the call site, leading to linker errors. Practice by instantiating MyStack for int and for std::string; you will see how the same blueprint yields two concrete classes. Takeaway: class templates give you powerful reusable containers, but you must consider type requirements and keep definitions available for instantiation.

Template instantiation is the process where the compiler generates concrete functions or classes from a generic template using the types you supply. Contrast this with a regular class: a non-template class has a single compiled form that the linker uses. For templates, the compiler waits until it knows which types you used and then produces a version for each unique set of template arguments. For example, using MyStack<int> and MyStack<std::string> produces two distinct classes at compile time. An important subtlety: the template definition must be visible when the compiler instantiates it; otherwise you get undefined reference or linker errors because the compiler couldn't generate the needed symbols. Another difference is code bloat risk — each instantiation produces separate code — but that is balanced by type safety and often better inlining. Misconception check: instantiation is not a runtime action; it happens during compilation. Practical takeaway: keep template definitions in headers and be deliberate about which instantiations you create to manage compile time and binary size. Instantiation: Template vs Regular Class means the compiler produces a concrete version of a template for each distinct set of template arguments used in code, at compile time.. In practical terms, how the compiler generates concrete code from templates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

One frequent pitfall is getting undefined reference linker errors when templates are declared in a header but defined in a separate. cpp file. The fundamental reason is that templates are instantiated where they are used, and the compiler must see the full template definition at that point to generate the concrete code. If only a declaration is visible, the compiler cannot produce the necessary instantiation and the linker cannot find the symbol. For beginners the simplest and most reliable solution is to place both declaration and definition in the header file so that any translation unit that uses the template has access to the full definition. Alternatives include explicit instantiation or including the. cpp at the bottom of the header, but these are more advanced techniques. A concrete scenario: you declare a LinkedList template in LinkedList. h but implement member functions in LinkedList. cpp. When main. cpp uses LinkedList, the compiler will not instantiate the methods because their definitions were not visible; the final link step reports undefined references. Misconception check: this is not a runtime bug — it is a compile/link-time visibility problem. Takeaway: keep template definitions available at the point of instantiation, typically by defining templates in headers.

Type deduction is the compiler's ability to infer template arguments from function call parameters. For many function templates you simply call the function and the compiler deduces the types automatically. For example, calling printValue(5) lets the compiler deduce T as int. However, deduction has limits. If argument types differ or if the call lacks enough information, the compiler cannot deduce a single type parameter and you must specify template arguments manually. For instance, a swap template requires both parameters to be the same deduced type; swap(1, 2.0) fails deduction. Another case is class templates where you must provide the type when you declare the object: MyStack s(10); here no deduction happens at the point of declaration. A common misconception is that deduction will magically convert or coerce types; it will not. It must find a single type that matches parameter types or you must supply explicit template parameters. Practical advice: rely on deduction for concise calls, but when you need mixed types or more control, declare explicit template arguments or use multiple template parameters. Question to consider: what rules guide the compiler's deduction when references, constness, or pointers are present?

Let's summarize the most important ideas. First, generic programming enables writing algorithms and structures that work independently of concrete types — templates are the mechanism for this in C++. Second, a template is a blueprint that uses placeholder types like T or T1 and T2; when you use a template with specific types the compiler generates concrete code. Third, function templates let you replace many similar overloads with a single implementation, relying on template argument deduction to make calls concise.
